075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark J: Psych is an American TV comedy-detective series (2006-2014) about Shawn Spencer, a private consultant so observant that he convinces the Santa Barbara police he is psychic. The show's running con raises real philosophical puzzles: when is lying justified if it catches killers, how can bad logic lead to true conclusions, and does Shawn's fluency in abduction, thin-slicing, and Gettier cases amount to knowledge? His hyper-observation turns every case into an epistemology lesson.
076 - The Good Wife and Philosophy - Tem: The Good Wife is an American legal drama (CBS, 2009-2016) about Alicia Florrick, who rebuilds a law career while standing by her politician husband after a prostitution scandal. Unlike older courtroom shows, it follows lawyers home, where compromises get personal. Its cases probe the ethics of zealous advocacy, drone warfare, utilitarian client-pleasing, Kantian duty versus an ethic of care, and what a woman owes her family, her lovers, and herself.
077 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy -: Boardwalk Empire is HBO's Prohibition-era crime drama (2010-2014), following Atlantic City treasurer and bootlegger Nucky Thompson through the world of Capone, Lucky Luciano, and corrupt G-men. A show about criminals who must lie, charm, and kill to hold power is naturally philosophical territory: the essays test Nucky against Machiavelli's Prince and Nietzsche's Superman, read Jimmy and Richard as veterans facing existential despair, and ask whether the docudrama itself misleads viewers about real history.
078 - Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My: Futurama is Matt Groening and David X. Cohen's animated sci-fi comedy (first aired 1999-2003, later revived), following delivery-boy Fry, frozen in 1999 and awakened in the year 3000. Behind the jokes it is a serious science-fiction show, and the essays use its episodes to argue about free will and self-government, flag burning and tolerating offensive speech, ecological waste, the ethics of war, and why 'perversion' is an arbitrary judgment. The mundane made strange does real philosophical work.
079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The: Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818) is the novel of a scientist who reanimates dead flesh and abandons his nameless creature, and its monster has since spread through hundreds of films, from Boris Karloff to Mel Brooks and Herman Munster. The story keeps earning philosophy because it condenses modern anxieties: is 'playing God' a real wrong, what do creators owe their creations, does the creature have a soul, and what does the 'Frankenfood' metaphor get right or wrong about biotechnology today?
080 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - Geno: Ender's Game is Orson Scott Card's 1985 science-fiction novel (filmed in 2013), in which gifted children are trained at a Battle School to fight an alien enemy, and child genius Ender unknowingly wipes out an entire species. The book's traps are philosophical: can an engineered childhood be justified, is Ender's empathy also his weapon, is he virtuous or a pawn of disciplinary power, and who bears responsibility when the game turns out to be xenocide?
081 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosop: How I Met Your Mother is an American sitcom (CBS, 2005-2014) framed as Ted telling his children the long, digressive story of how he met their mother. Its trick is making viewers love Barney, an appalling manipulator, and the essays take that seriously: why we empathize with fictional badness, whether Barney's 'be awesome instead' is a theory of emotion, if ethical egoism can survive the Bro Code, and how the show stages Sartrean bad faith and non-essentialist feminism through Robin.
082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The: Jurassic Park began as Michael Crichton's 1990 novel and became Spielberg's 1993 blockbuster: scientists clone dinosaurs for a theme park, and the park predictably collapses. Its heart is Malcolm's question, not 'could we' but 'should we', which the essays pursue through the ethics of de-extinction, whether frog-patched clones are really dinosaurs (a Ship of Theseus puzzle), what a botched 'intelligent design' suggests about designers, and whether Hammond's arrogance, not science itself, is the real villain.
083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nat: This book is not about a single show but about the Devil as a pop-culture figure: Hellraiser's Pinhead, The Devil's Advocate, the Rolling Stones' 'Sympathy for the Devil', demonic video-game villains, and Halloween folklore. Belief in Satan, the essays argue, deserves the same scrutiny as any other belief. They test whether the scales of justice require a Hell, ask what our names for the Devil fix in how we see him, and trace prophecy, free will, and bad faith through his many screen appearances.
084 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Var: Leonard Cohen (1934-2016) was a Canadian poet and novelist who became a beloved singer-songwriter, famous for 'Hallelujah' and a gravelly voice musing on love, loss, and faith. Because his songs sit oddly between high poetry and popular music, they invite philosophical questions: does the divide between high and popular art even hold? The essays read him through Stoicism and Pyrrhonian skepticism, Camus and Kierkegaard, Judith Butler on masculinity, and Hume on whether he was, in fact, a good singer.
